title: If I Could Turn Back Time
blurb: Talk about life events and choices

steps.html:
A man in London sold his records because his wife kept wishing he would. He is buying them back one album at a time, and the research says he is luckier than he feels.

  • Read about regret and what the evidence says
  • Use wish and if only for all three time frames
  • Talk about choices and their consequences
  • Write about a decision you would take differently

steps.title: Four things people phoned in to regret
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 148 words

A radio programme asked listeners for their regrets, and the same four kinds came back all morning.

The first was a decision not taken. A man in Glasgow had turned down his father's offer of money towards a flat, when property was still affordable. If only he had listened, he said. Twice.

The second was something said. A woman told a friend she had never understood the relationship anyway, and the friend went back to the boyfriend a week later. She wishes she could be less honest sometimes.

The third was something got rid of. A man in London sold his record collection because his wife kept saying she wished he would sell it. He is now buying it back, one album at a time.

The fourth was silence. A woman bullied at work for two years wishes she had said something, and would not tolerate it now.

steps.title: What people actually regret
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 146 words

The research on regret is consistent and mildly uncomfortable. In the short term, people regret the things they did. Over a lifetime, they regret the things they did not do, and by a wide margin.

The explanation offered is that an action produces a definite result you can examine, get used to and eventually forgive. An inaction produces nothing, so the imagination fills the gap with the best possible version, and it never has to compete with what actually happened.

This is why the man buying his records back is in a better position than he thinks. His regret has an object. He can spend forty pounds a month on it.

The regrets that last are the other kind: the course not taken, the thing not said, the year not spent somewhere else. Nobody can buy those back one album at a time.

steps.title: Answer the questions.
steps.prompt: What is the difference between short-term and lifetime regret?
options: In the short term people regret actions; over a lifetime they regret inactions.
The other way round: actions over a lifetime, inactions in the short term.
There is no measurable difference between the two time frames.
steps.answer: In the short term people regret actions; over a lifetime they regret inactions.

steps.title: What you want to be different
steps.html:
Three time frames, three forms, and the one that is not about time at all.

Wish + past simple = you want a present situation to be different. I wish I had more time. I wish I were taller. The past tense marks distance from reality, exactly as in the second conditional.

Wish + past perfect = you want a past event to have been different. She wishes she had said something at the time. This is regret.

Wish + would = you want somebody else to change a behaviour that annoys you. His wife kept saying she wished he would sell them. You cannot use it about yourself: I wish I would stop — say I wish I could stop.

Wish + could = an ability or possibility you do not have. She wishes she could be a little less honest.

If only works identically and is stronger: If only he had listened. If only I hadn't opened my mouth. It often stands alone, with no main clause at all.

The commonest error: using the present after wish. I wish I have more time. Every form after wish steps one back.

Same pattern as wish, different opener.

I wish I have more time.
The commonest error in this area.

steps.title: Four wishes about one record collection
steps.html:
1. The facts: he sold the records; he now wants them; his wife wanted him to sell them.
  2. About the past event: He wishes he hadn't sold them. Past perfect after wish.
  3. About the present situation: He wishes he still had them. Past simple after wish.
  4. About somebody else's behaviour, from her side at the time: She wished he would sell them. Would only for another person.
  5. About his own inability: He wishes he could afford to buy them all at once. Not wishes he would afford. And the strongest version of the first: If only he hadn't sold them.

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use wish in at least two different time frames, and if only at least once.
steps.html:
• Open with the decision and when you took it.
  • Separate the part you do not regret from the part you do.
  • Use <i>wish</i> about the past and <i>wish</i> about the present.
  • Use <i>if only</i> once.
  • Close by weighing the two.

Useful language

  • My biggest regret is …-ing
  • If only I had …
  • I wish I hadn't … / I wish I could …
  • I wish somebody would …
  • With hindsight, I should never have …
  • It turned out to be a blessing in disguise.
steps.modelHtml:
The course I didn't take

At twenty-two I was offered a place on a two-year programme in Warsaw, and I turned it down because my grandmother was ill and I was the only one at home. That part I do not regret. She died fourteen months later and I was there, which was worth more than any qualification.

What I regret is what I did afterwards, which was nothing. I wish I had applied again the following year. If only somebody had told me that the place was offered annually and that nobody would have thought less of me for asking twice.

I wish I could say the decision cost me nothing. It cost me about four years. But the research is right about one thing: I do not think about the fourteen months at all, and I think about the four years constantly.
